problemText: You are looking at a map for the first time. Near the top of the page, you see the words 'Mountain Valley State Park Map' printed in large letters. What is the name of this map part, and what question does it answer?
choices: It is the scale bar, and it answers the question 'About how big a distance on the map really is?'
It is the legend, and it answers the question 'What do these symbols and colors mean?'
It is the compass rose, and it answers the question 'Which way is north?'
It is the title, and it answers the question 'What does this whole map show?'
hints: The lesson teaches that printed words near the top of a map name what the map is about.
Remember that each map part answers its own question — this part answers a question about the map's subject.

problemText: A student finds a map with a small box containing a list: a green square paired with 'park,' a red line paired with 'road,' and a blue circle paired with 'pond.' The student wants to know what a red line represents on this map. Which part should the student use to find this answer?
choices: The legend, because it pairs each symbol and color with its meaning
The title, because it names the overall subject of the map
The compass rose, because it shows which way is north
The scale bar, because it shows how big distances really are
hints: The question is about what a symbol means on this particular map, not about direction or distance.
The lesson describes one part as 'a list that pairs each symbol with what that symbol stands for.'

problemText: You are hiking and you want to know about how far it is between two landmarks on your paper map. You look at the map and find a small straight bar near the bottom corner with marks showing '0' on the left and '2 miles' on the right. Why is this bar helpful for answering your question about distance?
choices: Because it shows you the names and locations of all the landmarks printed on the map
Because it translates a length on the page into a real-world distance you can understand
Because it explains which direction is north and where each landmark sits relative to that direction
Because it displays all the different symbols used on the map and what real-world features they represent
hints: The lesson says this part is 'the only one of the four parts that connects a length on the page to a distance in the real world.'
Think about what information you need to know if two landmarks are close together on paper but far apart in real life.

problemText: A student studying the Riverside Campground Map sees a small drawing with an arrow labeled N pointing toward the left edge of the page, with three shorter lines branching off to show the other directions. Another student claims, 'A picnic table symbol sits directly above a stream symbol on this page, so the picnic table must be north of the stream.' Is the second student correct, and why or why not?
choices: Yes, the student is correct, because page position always matches cardinal direction regardless of how the map is rotated or printed
Yes, the student is correct, because the legend identifies what each symbol means and confirms the picnic table symbol's location
No, the student is incorrect, because the compass rose shows that north points left, not up, so directly above means west, not north
No, the student is incorrect, because the scale bar measures distance between locations rather than showing directions
hints: Remember that the compass rose tells you which real-world direction matches each location on this particular map page.
The lesson warns: 'On this page, directly above cannot mean anything but north' only if north points to the top — but what if the compass rose points a different direction?

problemText: A student wants to find out three pieces of information from the Eagle Ridge Trail Map: (1) what the whole map shows, (2) what a purple star symbol means on this map, and (3) which cardinal directions are shown. For each piece of information, which single map part would the student need to check?
choices: The scale bar for (1), the compass rose for (2), and the legend for (3)
The legend for (1), the scale bar for (2), and the title for (3)
The compass rose for (1), the title for (2), and the scale bar for (3)
The title for (1), the legend for (2), and the compass rose for (3)
hints: Match each question to the part built to answer it: what-is-this-map, what-does-this-symbol-mean, and which-way-is-which.

Recall that the lesson teaches: 'A question about the map's overall subject' goes with one part, 'a question about what a symbol means' goes with another, and 'a question about which way' goes with a third.

problemText: A hiker compares two different maps of nearby areas. On Map A, a town symbol sits in the exact center of the page, and the compass rose shows N pointing upward. On Map B, the same town symbol sits in the exact center of the page, but the compass rose shows N pointing to the right. If both maps show the same area of the real world, why is the town's position relative to north different between the two maps, and what does this teach you about reading direction on any map?
choices: The pages are turned different ways; every map's own compass rose determines which direction is north for that particular page, not memory or habit
The scale bars on the two maps are different sizes; this difference in scale affects how directions are measured and displayed on each map
The town moved between when Map A and Map B were made; north always points to the top of any page and locations cannot change on a map
The legends on the two maps use different symbols; the symbols chosen determine what cardinal directions will point to on that particular map
hints: The compass rose is described in the lesson as the part that shows 'which way is north' — for that particular map.

The lesson includes a warning: 'Always read the compass rose printed on the map in front of you,' and gives an example of how the same page position means different real-world directions on different maps.

problemText: A map's legend shows country borders marked with black lines and capital cities marked with a star inside a circle. What main job is this map built to do?
choices: Show the human-made boundaries and place names of countries
Show how high or low the land sits in different areas
Show how one kind of data, such as rainfall, spreads across the region
Show the names of all rivers and mountains in the area
hints: Look at what the legend actually lists — borders and capital cities are what kind of information?
Remember: the three map types are built around different purposes. Which purpose does a legend of borders and capitals serve?

problemText: A map's legend lists these three entries: dark green for elevation from sea level to 500 feet, tan for elevation from 500 to 2,000 feet, and gray-brown for elevation above 2,000 feet. No country borders or rainfall data appear on the legend. What kind of map is this, and why?
choices: A political map, because it uses three different colors to show three different countries
A physical map, because its colors show elevation, the height of the land at different places
A thematic map, because it spreads information across an area using different colors
A thematic map, because the three colors represent three different kinds of geographical data
hints: What does each color on this legend stand for — elevation or something else?
Recall: a physical map's colors specifically represent how high or low the land is. Do the colors here match that job?

problemText: A student is looking at a map with colors showing which areas grow mostly coffee, which grow mostly cocoa, and which grow mostly sugar cane. The student says this must be a physical map because it uses colors to show differences across the land. What is the error in the student's reasoning?
choices: The student confused what the colors represent with the fact that colors exist; since the legend shows crop types rather than elevation or landforms, this is a thematic map focused on one data topic

The student incorrectly assumed that using any colors at all makes a map physical, when in fact the legend determines the type based on whether it lists natural features, boundaries, or one chosen data theme
The student judged the map by the fact that colors were used, not by what the colors stand for; the map is thematic, showing one chosen data topic spread across an area
The student failed to recognize that the legend shows agricultural products spread across regions, which makes this a thematic map built to display how one kind of data varies from place to place
hints: What do the colors actually represent on this map — elevation, or something else?
The key rule from the lesson: never choose a map type by noticing colors are used; instead, ask what those colors stand for.

problemText: Three different maps all show the same country. Map A's legend lists country borders and capital cities. Map B's legend lists colors showing elevation from low to high and symbols for rivers and mountain peaks. Map C's legend lists colors showing how population is distributed across different regions. Which statement correctly describes what each map is built to do?
choices: Map A shows natural landforms, Map B shows boundaries, and Map C shows where people live in larger numbers
Map A shows climate zones, Map B shows natural features, and Map C shows country borders
Map A shows elevation, Map B shows boundaries, and Map C shows rainfall patterns
Map A shows boundaries and place names, Map B shows the natural shape of the land, and Map C shows how one kind of data spreads across the area
hints: For each map, look at what its legend actually lists and match it to the three main jobs: showing boundaries, showing natural land shape, or showing one data topic spread across an area.
Remember: the same place can appear on all three kinds of maps, each one built around a different legend answering a different question.

problemText: A geographer wants to help city planners understand which areas in a region would be easiest to build roads through based on how steep or flat the land is. The planner asks to see a map. Which type of map should the geographer choose, and which feature of that map's legend would give the answer?
choices: A physical map, using colors that show elevation to identify flat versus steep areas
A thematic map showing population density, because more populated areas have better roads already built
A political map, using the capital city symbols to mark the best route
A thematic map showing rainfall, because dry areas are easier to build roads in
hints: To plan road building, what information about the land matters most — its borders, its height, or rainfall?
Which map type's legend is built to show how high or low the land sits in different places?

problemText: A student examines two different maps of the same forest region. Both maps use green color across most of the area, but the legends are different. On Map 1, the legend says green stands for elevation between 1,000 and 3,000 feet. On Map 2, the legend says green stands for areas where oak trees are the most common species. Explain why these two maps are different types despite both using green in the same places, and identify each type.
choices: Map 1 is physical because it shows elevation as a natural feature, and Map 2 is political because it identifies specific plant boundaries even though it uses the same green color in those regions
Map 1 is physical and Map 2 is thematic because the colors stand for different things — elevation versus one chosen data topic — even though the color itself is the same
Map 1 is thematic and Map 2 is physical because Map 1 focuses on height data while Map 2 displays a natural feature like vegetation distribution across the landscape

Map 1 represents land height using green to show elevation ranges, while Map 2 uses green to show where a single tree species dominates, making them different types because their legends show different purposes even if the color appearance is identical
hints: The lesson teaches that the type of map is decided by what the legend lists, not by what color is used or what it looks like.
On Map 1, what do the colors represent? On Map 2, what do the same colors represent? How does that difference change the map type?

problemText: According to the seven-continent convention used in this lesson, which one of the following is a continent? Remember that a continent is one of Earth's largest continuous areas of land.
choices: The Arctic Ocean
Antarctica
Greenland
The Atlantic Ocean
hints: A continent is land, not water.
Look for the largest continuous area of land, not an ocean or an island that is not counted as a continent on its own.

problemText: You are looking at a globe and you can see that North America touches both the Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean. According to what the lesson taught about the four oceans and their positions, which direction would you look from North America to find the Atlantic Ocean?
choices: North
West
East
South
hints: The Atlantic Ocean lies between the Americas on one side and Europe and Africa on the other side of the globe.
Think about which side of North America faces toward Europe — that is the direction you would travel across the Atlantic Ocean to reach Europe.

problemText: A geographer describes Europe's position by saying: 'Europe has Asia to its east, and the Atlantic Ocean to its west.' Using the two-question routine taught in the lesson, which of the following checks whether this description is correct by flipping one of the statements?
choices: If Asia is east of Europe, then Asia must also be north of Europe.
If Europe has the Atlantic Ocean to its west, then the Atlantic Ocean must have land to its east.
If Europe is east of Asia, then it cannot also be west of the Atlantic Ocean.
If Europe has Asia to its east, then Asia must have Europe to its west.
hints: The lesson taught that you can flip a position statement to check it — read the relationship from the other side, and it should come out flipped but never contradicted.
When you flip a direction, east becomes west and west becomes east, but the two places stay connected.

problemText: The lesson states that Africa, Europe, and Asia are counted as three separate continents even though they sit on one continuous landmass with no water between them. Australia, by contrast, is an island continent surrounded entirely by ocean. Based on the two-question routine taught in the lesson, what is one key difference in the answer you would give to the first question — 'what does this continent touch along its edges?' — when comparing Australia to Europe?
choices: Europe touches at least one other continent, but Australia touches only oceans on all sides.
Europe touches only water bodies, while Australia touches both other continents and oceans at different points along its border.
Europe is separated from other continents by small seas, but Australia is isolated from other continents by vast oceans only.
Europe has land borders with neighboring continents, but Australia has no land borders with any other continent.
hints: The first question asks what touches a continent along its edges — could be other continents or could be oceans.
Think about the lesson's point that Australia has no land connection to any other continent, while Europe sits on a shared landmass.

problemText: A student learns that the Pacific Ocean is the largest of the four oceans and lies between the Americas on one side and Asia and Australia on the other. The student then tries to describe the Pacific Ocean's position using the two-question routine: 'The Pacific Ocean touches North America to its east, South America to its southeast, Asia to its west, and Australia to its southwest.' Why is this description incomplete, and what should the student have included?
choices: The student gave directions that were too specific (southeast and southwest) instead of using only the four main directions (north, south, east, west).
The student forgot to mention that the Arctic Ocean lies to the north of the Pacific Ocean, which is a neighbor that touches its edges.
The student listed too many neighbors; the Pacific Ocean touches only one ocean and one continent, not four places.
The student included South America when he should have included Central America, because Central America is more important to the Pacific Ocean's position.
hints: Reread the lesson's description of what borders the Arctic Ocean and what borders the Pacific Ocean — do they touch each other?
The two-question routine asks what touches a place along its edges; think about whether the Arctic Ocean's southern edge might touch the Pacific Ocean's northern edge.

problemText: The lesson explains that geographers do not all divide the world the same way, and gives two examples of different conventions: some count six continents instead of seven, and some name a fifth ocean (the Southern Ocean) instead of four. Based on what the lesson taught about how and why continents are separated, which of the following best explains why a geographer might choose to combine Europe and Asia into one continent instead of counting them separately?
choices: Because Europe and Asia are closer to each other than any other pair of continents, making them more similar to each other than to their other neighbors.
Because the Arctic Ocean is so small and cold that it does not separate Europe from Asia the way larger oceans separate other continents.
Because Europe and Asia sit on one continuous landmass with no ocean between them, even though the lesson's convention still counts them as two separate continents for practical reasons.
Because the Indian Ocean lies between Europe and Asia, and using the Indian Ocean as a boundary is easier than drawing an invisible line through land.
hints: The lesson specifically taught that Europe and Asia are joined on one landmass with no water between them — this is a fact about how they are actually connected on Earth.

Think about what reason a geographer might have for counting them as one continent instead of two — would it relate to how they are physically connected, or to how far apart they are, or to how similar their weather is?

problemText: What is a hemisphere? Use the word parts to explain what the term means.
choices: The area near the North Pole and the South Pole
A line that runs around the middle of Earth from east to west
Half of Earth, because hemi means half and sphere means ball
One of the four imaginary lines that people agreed to draw on maps
hints: The lesson breaks down the word into two parts: hemi and sphere.
Think about what each word part means on its own before combining them.

problemText: A location sits south of the Equator and east of the Prime Meridian. Which two hemispheres contain this location?
choices: Northern Hemisphere and Eastern Hemisphere
Northern Hemisphere and Western Hemisphere
Southern Hemisphere and Western Hemisphere
Southern Hemisphere and Eastern Hemisphere
hints: Remember to answer question 1 first: is the place north or south of the Equator?
Then answer question 2: is the place east or west of the Prime Meridian?

problemText: Which imaginary line separates the Eastern Hemisphere from the Western Hemisphere?
choices: The Prime Meridian, which runs from the North Pole to the South Pole through Greenwich
The Equator, which runs from the North Pole to the South Pole and divides east from west
The International Date Line, which runs east and west around the widest part of Earth
The Tropic of Cancer, which runs from the North Pole to the South Pole and marks the hemisphere boundary
hints: Think about which line creates the east-west pair of hemispheres.
The correct line passes through a specific city in England.

problemText: A plane is flying north and crosses the Equator. A few hours later, it flies west and crosses the Prime Meridian. Based on these movements alone, which two hemispheres is the plane now in?
choices: Southern Hemisphere and Western Hemisphere
Northern Hemisphere and Western Hemisphere
Northern Hemisphere and Eastern Hemisphere
Southern Hemisphere and Eastern Hemisphere
hints: When you cross a line while heading in a direction, you end up on that side of the line. Crossing while flying north puts you north of the line.
Work through both questions in order: first the Equator crossing, then the Prime Meridian crossing.

problemText: A student claims that South America is only in the Southern Hemisphere. Explain what is wrong with this statement using the two-question method taught in the lesson.
choices: The student did not know that South America is larger than most other continents
The student forgot that the Prime Meridian runs through South America, so it must also be in the Western Hemisphere
The student answered only question 1 and never ran question 2 about east or west of the Prime Meridian
The student did not realize that the Equator does not actually divide South America into two parts
hints: Every place on Earth should be named by answering two questions in order.
The student only answered the first question about north or south, but skipped checking east or west.

problemText: The Equator runs across the middle of Africa, and the Prime Meridian runs down through its western part. Based on this information and the lesson rules, how many hemispheres contain land from Africa?
choices: Two hemispheres, because Africa straddles the Equator but lies mostly on one side of the Prime Meridian
Two hemispheres, because every place on Earth sits in exactly two hemispheres
Three hemispheres, because the Prime Meridian splits Africa into eastern and western parts while the Equator creates northern and southern divisions
All four hemispheres, because both lines cross the continent and divide it into parts that belong to different halves
hints: A single point sits in two hemispheres, but a whole continent can span more than one of each pair.
When both lines cross a continent, think about what lands exist on each side of each line.
